title: Meetings — agenda, proposals and minutes
goal: Take part in an Indonesian meeting from the opening formula to the closing one: follow the agenda, interrupt politely, make a proposal and agree to one — and then turn what was said into proper written minutes.
bekal: open, steer and close a meeting with fixed phrases like *rapat saya buka* and *izin menyela*
use the word families of *usul* and *setuju*: *mengusulkan, usulan, menyetujui, disetujui, persetujuan*
rewrite casual speech as minutes: *Bu Ratna bilang…* → *Ibu Ratna menyampaikan bahwa…*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rapat di balai desa
dialogs.intro: A Tuesday morning in May at the balai desa, the village hall. Pak Harun chairs the monthly project meeting; around the table sit Sarah, Dr. Lestari, Bu Ratna and — taking notes at the end — Yoga.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Bapak-Ibu sekalian, karena sudah pukul sembilan, rapat ini saya buka.
lines.id: Ladies and gentlemen, as it is nine o'clock, I declare this meeting open.
lines.literal: Sir-Madam all, because already o'clock nine, meeting this I open.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Pak. Agenda hari ini ada tiga: laporan perbaikan, papan petunjuk, dan festival desa.
lines.id: Thank you. There are three items on today's agenda: the repair report, the signposts, and the village festival.
lines.literal: receive love, Sir. agenda day this exist three: report repair, board direction, and festival village.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Silakan dimulai dari laporan perbaikan, Mbak Sarah.
lines.id: Please start with the repair report, Sarah.
lines.literal: please be-started from report repair, miss Sarah.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dari dua belas rumah yang rusak, sepuluh sudah selesai diperbaiki. Sisanya masih menunggu bahan bangunan.
lines.id: Of the twelve damaged houses, ten have been repaired. The rest are still waiting for building materials.
lines.literal: from two ten house which damaged, ten already finished be-repaired. rest-its still wait material building.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Izin menyela, Pak. Homestay saya termasuk yang dua itu, padahal tamu sudah pesan untuk bulan Juni.
lines.id: Sorry to interrupt. My homestay is one of those two, and guests have already booked for June.
lines.literal: permission interrupt, Sir. homestay my included which two that, whereas guest already order for month June.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Baik, dicatat. Itu kita jadikan prioritas. Agenda kedua?
lines.id: Noted. We'll make that a priority. Second item?
lines.literal: good, is-noted. that we make priority. agenda second?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Saya usul papan petunjuk dibuat dalam dua bahasa, Indonesia dan Inggris.
lines.id: I propose that the signposts be made in two languages, Indonesian and English.
lines.literal: I propose board direction be-made in two language, Indonesia and English.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Kalau bisa tiga, Bu. Bahasa Jawa juga, biar tamu ikut belajar.
lines.id: Three, if possible. Javanese too, so that visitors learn a bit as well.
lines.literal: if can three, Madam. language Java also, so-that guest join learn.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Usulan yang menarik. Tapi anggarannya cukup, Mbak Sarah?
lines.id: An interesting proposal. But is the budget enough, Sarah?
lines.literal: proposal which interesting. but budget-the enough, miss Sarah?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Cukup untuk dua bahasa. Untuk tiga, kita perlu tambahan sekitar dua juta rupiah.
lines.id: Enough for two languages. For three we'd need about two million rupiah more.
lines.literal: enough for two language. for three, we need addition around two million rupiah.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Bagaimana, Bapak-Ibu? Apakah usul tiga bahasa dapat disetujui?
lines.id: What do you all think? Can the three-language proposal be approved?
lines.literal: how, Sir-Madam? whether proposal three language can be-approved?

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Setuju, Pak. Kelompok homestay siap urunan untuk kekurangannya.
lines.id: Agreed. The homestay group is ready to chip in to cover the shortfall.
lines.literal: agree, Sir. group homestay ready chip-in for shortage-the.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Kalau begitu, disepakati tiga bahasa. Tindak lanjutnya, Mbak Sarah menghubungi percetakan.
lines.id: In that case, three languages it is. As a follow-up, Sarah will contact the printer.
lines.literal: if like-that, is-agreed three language. follow-up-its, miss Sarah contact printing-house.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Siap, Pak. Minggu depan hasilnya saya laporkan.
lines.id: Will do. I'll report back next week.
lines.literal: ready, Sir. week front result-the I report.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Agenda festival kita bahas pada rapat berikutnya. Rapat saya tutup. Terima kasih.
lines.id: We'll discuss the festival at the next meeting. I declare the meeting closed. Thank you.
lines.literal: agenda festival we discuss at meeting next. meeting I close. receive love.

notes: **Rapat ini saya buka / Rapat saya tutup** — the chair's fixed formulas, both in the “thing + person + verb” passive you know from A1. In more ceremonial meetings the chair then knocks the table three times with a small gavel (*ketok palu*), and *sudah diketok palu* has become slang for “officially decided”.

**Izin menyela** — “permission to interrupt”. Indonesians rarely just cut in at a meeting; they ask first, even if they then carry on without waiting for an answer. *Mohon izin, Pak* is the more formal version, *Maaf, boleh saya tambahkan?* the gentler one.
**Dicatat** — “(it is) noted”. The chair says it to show a point has been heard without promising anything yet. *Kita jadikan prioritas* — “we make it a priority” — is the promise.

**Usul vs usulan.** Both mean “a proposal”, and Dr. Lestari uses both. *Saya usul…* works like a verb in speech (“I suggest…”); the formal verb is *mengusulkan*. *Usulan* is always a noun: *usulan yang menarik*.

**Disetujui vs disepakati.** *Setuju* is agreement by one person or a vote; *sepakat* is agreement reached together, by consensus. When Pak Harun says *disepakati*, he signals that the room decided as one — the Indonesian ideal of *musyawarah untuk mufakat* (see Section 2).

**Urunan** — everyone chipping in money for a shared cost; *patungan* is the same thing in Jakarta. *Tindak lanjut* (follow-up) is the word you will see in every set of minutes; *menindaklanjuti* is “to follow up”.

grammars.title: The meeting, from start to finish
body: Indonesian meetings run on a small set of formulas. The chair uses the most formal ones; participants can be a notch lighter.

head: Moment
Indonesian
English
rows: *Silakan, Bu Ratna. / Waktu dan tempat kami persilakan.*
Go ahead. / The floor is yours.
*Izin menyela. / Mohon maaf, boleh saya tambahkan?*
Sorry to interrupt. / May I add something?
What do you think? Can we agree?
In that case, it's agreed… / It is decided that…
*Rapat saya tutup. Terima kasih atas kehadirannya.*
The meeting is closed. Thank you for coming.

after: *Waktu dan tempat kami persilakan* — “we invite (you to) the time and the place” — sounds odd in English but is the standard formal way to hand the microphone to someone.
⚠️ Do not answer a chair's *Bagaimana?* with a flat *Tidak setuju*. See Unit 7: *Saya kurang setuju* or *Mungkin bisa dipertimbangkan lagi* is how disagreement sounds in a room like this.

grammars.title: Two word families you will use every meeting
body: *Usul* and *setuju* each grow into a whole family. The prefixes do exactly what they did in A2, so you can build most of these yourself.
after: Notice the difference: you are *setuju dengan* a person or idea, but you *menyetujui* a proposal or a budget — a formal act. *Saya setuju dengan Bu Ratna*, but *Kepala desa menyetujui anggaran itu*.
*Agar* (“so that”) after *mengusulkan* is followed by a plain clause: *Saya mengusulkan agar papan dibuat dalam tiga bahasa.*

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Yoga menulis notulen
dialogs.intro: That afternoon, at the project's little office in the village, Yoga has typed up the minutes. He asks Sarah to look them over before they go to Pak Harun.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Mbak, notulennya udah jadi. Tolong dicek, ya. Aku nulisnya sambil ngantuk, sih.
lines.id: Sarah, the minutes are done. Could you check them? I was half asleep when I wrote them, mind you.
lines.literal: miss, minutes-the already done. please be-checked, [ya]. I write-it while sleepy, [sih].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke. Hmm, “Bu Ratna bilang homestay-nya belum beres.” Ini terlalu santai untuk notulen.
lines.id: OK. Hmm, “Bu Ratna said her homestay isn't sorted yet.” This is too casual for minutes.
lines.literal: OK. hmm, Mrs Ratna say homestay-her not-yet sorted. this too relaxed for minutes.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Terus harusnya gimana, Mbak?
lines.id: So how should it go?
lines.literal: then should-it how, miss?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Misalnya: “Ibu Ratna menyampaikan bahwa dua homestay belum selesai diperbaiki.”
lines.id: For example: “Mrs Ratna reported that two homestays have not yet been fully repaired.”
lines.literal: for-example: Madam Ratna convey that two homestay not-yet finished be-repaired.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Wah, kaku banget. Tapi oke, aku ganti.
lines.id: Wow, that's stiff. But fine, I'll change it.
lines.literal: wow, stiff very. but OK, I change.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terus, keputusan jangan dicampur dengan diskusi. Tulis di poin tersendiri.
lines.id: Also, don't mix the decisions in with the discussion. Put them under a separate point.
lines.literal: then, decision don't be-mixed with discussion. write at point separate.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Jadi “Keputusan: papan petunjuk dibuat dalam tiga bahasa”, gitu?
lines.id: So “Decision: signposts to be made in three languages”, like that?
lines.literal: so decision: board direction be-made in three language, like-that?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul. Lalu tambahkan penanggung jawab dan tenggat untuk setiap tindak lanjut.
lines.id: Exactly. Then add the person responsible and a deadline for every follow-up.
lines.literal: correct. then add bearer responsibility and deadline for every follow-up.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Penanggung jawabnya Mbak Sarah, tenggatnya Senin depan. Mantap.
lines.id: Person responsible: you. Deadline: next Monday. Sorted.
lines.literal: bearer responsibility-the miss Sarah, deadline-the Monday front. solid.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jangan senang dulu. Kamu yang antar notulennya ke Pak Harun untuk ditandatangani.
lines.id: Don't celebrate yet. You're the one taking the minutes to Pak Harun to be signed.
lines.literal: don't happy first. you who deliver minutes-the to Mr Harun for be-signed.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Waduh. Siap, Mbak.
lines.id: Oh no. Will do.
lines.literal: [waduh]. ready, miss.

notes: **Notulen** (from Dutch *notulen*) is the minutes of a meeting; the person who writes them is the *notulis*. Some offices say *risalah rapat* in very formal documents. You *membuat* or *menyusun notulen*.

**Tolong dicek** — a request in the passive: “please (let it) be checked”. It sounds softer than *Tolong cek* because it does not point at the other person. Yoga's *sih* at the end is a shrug: “just so you know”.
**Beres** — “sorted, in order, done”, extremely common in speech: *Sudah beres?* (all sorted?), *Beres, Bos!* (consider it done). In writing it becomes *selesai* or *tuntas*.

**Menyampaikan** — “to convey, to pass on” — is the minutes-and-speeches replacement for *bilang*. Also useful: *menanyakan* (asked about), *menjelaskan* (explained), *mengusulkan* (proposed), *menanggapi* (responded).

**Penanggung jawab** (the person responsible, literally “bearer of the answer”) and **tenggat** (deadline) are the two columns every follow-up table needs. *Tenggat waktu* is the full form; in offices you will hear the English *deadline* just as often.
**Waduh** is a small groan of dismay, like “oh no” or “uh-oh”; *aduh* is its everyday sibling. *Mantap* — “solid, great” — is Yoga's all-purpose approval word.

grammars.title: From what was said to what is written
body: Minutes report speech in the third person, in standard Indonesian, with no slang and with names given their full title. The table shows the most common swaps.
after: *Sdr.* (*Saudara*) and *Sdri.* (*Saudari*) are the neutral written titles for a younger man or woman who is not a *Bapak* or *Ibu*: *Sdr. Yoga*.
*Berhalangan hadir* — “was prevented from attending” — is the kind way to record an absence without giving (or inventing) a reason.

blocks.text: Indonesian offices, schools and even RT meetings keep minutes in a very predictable shape. If you ever have to write one, fill in these headings in this order.

head: Heading
English
Example
rows: one short paragraph per agenda item

blocks.text: *Terlampir* means “attached” — you will meet it in every formal letter too. Times use a full stop, not a colon: *09.00*, and the time zone for Java is *WIB* (Western Indonesia Time).

Indonesia's ideal way of deciding is not a vote but *musyawarah untuk mufakat* — discussion until consensus, written into the fourth principle of Pancasila. In practice a chair will keep talking, rephrasing and asking *Bagaimana?* until nobody objects out loud. A vote (*pemungutan suara*, or simply *voting*) is a fallback, and can even feel slightly like a failure.

blocks.title: Reading the silence
items: Silence after *Bagaimana, Bapak-Ibu?* usually means agreement, but not always. Watch for *Ya… bisa saja, sih* — often a polite “no”.
Real objections tend to come later, in private, over coffee. A good coordinator checks with key people before the meeting, so that the meeting only confirms.

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

First, pumps to suck out the remaining water. Second, cement and sand to repair the houses.
*Pertama, pompa untuk menyedot sisa air. Kedua, semen dan pasir untuk perbaikan rumah.*
So how much money do you need, and what for?

And if the flood comes again?
